solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Rich, wants a country landscape feature that isn't laughingly odd (5,2-2)

blocks.note: that's rich means that's amusing, said of a claim too good to let pass

blocks.clueFragment: a country landscape feature that isn't
blocks.note: a ha-ha is the ditch sunk across an estate lawn to keep the deer out, a barrier that is not there to look at

explanation.surface: A wealthy landowner shopping for a garden feature nobody will laugh at.
explanation.walkthrough: Rich wants to be money and means amusing, as in that's rich. The ha-ha is an English estate's invisible fence, a wall dropped into a trench so the view from the house runs on unbroken.
explanation.definitionFit: Funny ha-ha is the phrase that picks out the amusing kind of funny as against funny peculiar, so it is oddness that raises a laugh.

clue.text: Not up to being featured in Sun? A blessing! (6)

indicators.note: To be featured in something is to appear inside it, so the letters wanted are sitting inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: six letters running straight on across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A tabloid running a piece on something providential.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and the exclamation are put in to break the run of letters into separate outbursts. Sun is the tabloid in the sentence and just a word to read through in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone not up to a job is unable to do it, the phrase and the word naming the same shortfall of capacity.

clue.text: Bust, if not pert is a nice turn-up for the books (3,6)

definitions.text: a nice turn-up for the books

indicators.note: Something bust is broken, and broken letters do not stay in the order they were printed in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A chest that has lost its firmness turning out to be a welcome surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: Bust is the joke and the instruction at once: broke, in the surface's money sense, and broken, in the wordplay's. A turn-up for the books is British for an unexpected result, and the books here are the accounts.
explanation.definitionFit: A turn-up for the books is an unlooked-for windfall, and the figure at the foot of a company's accounts is what turns up there when the year has gone well.

clue.text: Getting runs in the midst of confusion is cruel (5)

indicators.note: To be in the midst of a thing is to sit in the middle of it, so the letter lands inside the word named.

blocks.note: to make a hash of something is to make a confusion of it, and the word parts in the middle
r is how runs are entered in a cricket scorebook

explanation.surface: Picking up runs while everything around is chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: Runs is the cricket scorer's letter rather than the athletics verb, and the hash is the mess a cook makes of a dish rather than anything smoked.
explanation.definitionFit: A harsh sentence or a harsh word is a cruel one, the sense of needless severity rather than of a rough noise.

clue.text: Guy gets awfully hot for gung-ho Christian (7)

indicators.note: Awfully says the letters beside it have been badly treated, and badly treated letters come out in a new order.

blocks.note: a guy is a he, the pronoun standing in for the man
anagram fodder, four letters as printed
H is the letter on the hot tap

explanation.surface: Some bloke running a terrible temperature on behalf of a zealous believer.
explanation.walkthrough: Pete Hegseth is Trump's defense secretary, an evangelical who has staged prayer services at the Pentagon, which is what the definition is aimed at. The fodder arrives as three separate scraps rather than one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Hegseth wears his faith as loudly as his appetite for a war, so the gung-ho Christian is the man himself.

clue.text: Casually sat on member to make an impression (5)

indicators.note: Doing a thing casually is doing it with no care for the proper order, so those letters are set down in any order they like.

blocks.note: the three letters of sat, put down in another order
MP is a Member of Parliament, the member of most British clues

explanation.surface: Someone lounging on a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Member is the Commons abbreviation and, this being Private Eye, the anatomical joke as well. The impression is the mark pressed into wax or ink, not the one made at a party.
explanation.definitionFit: To stamp something is to press a mark into it, which is making an impression in the literal, inky sense.

clue.text: Stimulant forced into Conservative leader (5)

indicators.note: To force a thing is to work it out of its natural shape, and letters out of shape no longer sit in their printed order.
The leader of a word is the letter at its head, so that one is taken and the rest left.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, the four letters of the clue's own preposition
the letter at the head of Conservative

explanation.surface: A pick-me-up pressed on the Tory leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading forced into as an insertion: into is not joining the halves of the clue, it is the fodder. A tonic is a bracing medicine before it is the mixer in a gin.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonic is a drink or medicine taken to brace you up, which is a stimulant in the old chemist's-shop sense.

clue.text: "Avoid bonk," said wrongly (8)

blocks.note: to miss a thing is to avoid it, or to fail to meet it
both are blunt British words for sex

explanation.surface: An instruction to keep away from casual sex, badly phrased.
explanation.walkthrough: Said wrongly sits exactly where a homophone instruction would sit, and no sound is involved anywhere in this clue. A politician who has misspoken has usually said just what they meant.
explanation.definitionFit: To misspeak is to say the wrong thing, and the past tense is the form an apology reaches for: he misspoke.

clue.text: Sex partner with a new spur is flop (3,2,3)

blocks.note: a lay is a coarse word for whoever you go to bed with
the clue's own letter, taken as it stands
n is the standard short form for new
to egg someone on is to spur them on

explanation.surface: A bedmate whose fresh encouragement comes to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Egg on for spur is the piece that hides best, because the surface has already put birds out of mind. The phrase is American theatre slang for a show that dies in front of an audience.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay an egg is to fail flat in public, which is what a show does when it flops.

clue.text: See 16dn.
Joy's end shaking in see-through material (8)

indicators.note: A thing being shaken will not keep its parts in the order they went in, so those letters come out rearranged.
In puts what comes before it inside what comes after, so the shaken letters land within the longer word.

blocks.note: glass is the see-through material, and it parts after its third letter
the three letters of end in another order

explanation.surface: The last of the joy trembling behind a transparent screen.
explanation.walkthrough: Joy's end reads as the death of happiness and is really a three-letter word to shuffle. Material wants to be a fabric until see-through is allowed to settle it.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladness is the noun for being glad, a quieter word than joy for the same happiness.

clue.text: Pop band to get a new leader? Insult! (4)

indicators.note: A word's leader is the letter out in front, so getting a new one swaps that first letter for another.

blocks.note: Blur are the Britpop band of Parklife and Country House

explanation.surface: A chart act casting about for a new frontman.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue never says which letter arrives; the definition does, since only one substitute leaves a word that means an insult. Blur's actual leader is Damon Albarn, which is where the surface is looking.
explanation.definitionFit: A slur is a remark that blackens someone's name, an insult with a bit of stick left in it.

clue.text: Animal desire follows husband around initially (5)

indicators.note: What follows something comes along behind it, so this piece is written in after the one it follows.
Initially takes a word at its start, which is its first letter and nothing else.

blocks.note: H is the standard short form for husband, as on a form
a yen for something is a longing for it
the first letter of around, taken on its own

explanation.surface: A man trailed by his own appetites wherever he goes.
explanation.walkthrough: Yen is the longing before it is the Japanese money, and the last letter comes out of the word around itself rather than out of anything it describes. The animal wanted is the one whose call sounds like laughter.
explanation.definitionFit: The hyena is the scavenging dog-like animal of the African plains, so the bare word Animal is definition by category.

clue.text: Contraceptive financial limit (3)

blocks.note: the barrier device a woman fits before sex, known in Britain as the Dutch one
a ceiling set on spending, on benefits or on a rate

explanation.surface: A spending limit imposed on birth control.
explanation.walkthrough: Three letters and two senses, with no wordplay between them to mark the join: the definitions simply sit side by side. Reading them as one phrase about a budget is what the setter is counting on.
explanation.definitionFit: A cap is the rubber barrier fitted over the cervix, and a cap on wages is the ceiling set over spending — the same idea clamped on top.

clue.text: Possibly that of Beethoven .2? (5)

blocks.note: the symphony that opens on the four most famous notes in music
the decimal for one part in five

explanation.surface: A quiz-sheet shorthand pointing at one of Beethoven's works.
explanation.walkthrough: Possibly is the fairness marker: Beethoven wrote nine symphonies and only one of them answers here. The dot is not punctuation but a decimal point, and 0.2 is one part in five.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's Fifth is the symphony everyone can hum, and .2 is a fifth written as a decimal, so both halves name the same ordinal.

clue.text: (&10ac.) Dithering defector, a fool pocketing a lot of money – just what the electorate needs at present? (4-4)

definitions.text: just what the electorate needs at present

indicators.note: To dither is to shift about without ever settling, and letters that will not settle come out in a different order.
To pocket a thing is to take it in and keep it, so the money named finishes up inside the letters that took it.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters
a G is a grand, a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: A wavering turncoat and an idiot quietly trousering a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: The thirteen letters and the G are shuffled together, so the money is swallowed rather than slipped inside anything you could name. The phrase is the pollsters' term for the mood that decides elections when policy does not.
explanation.definitionFit: The feel-good factor is the sense of prosperity and optimism a government tries to conjure before a vote, which is what the clue says voters are short of.

clue.text: Endless money and electronic car ... and bathtime ejaculation (6)

indicators.note: Endless means the finish is missing, so the word arrives without the letter it ends on.

blocks.note: the euro is the money, and endless takes its final letter away
e is the letter stuck on e-mail and e-bike, the standard short form for electronic
the Ka is Ford's smallest hatchback, a two-letter gift to setters

explanation.surface: Leftover cash and an electric runabout, then a shout from the bath.
explanation.walkthrough: Ejaculation is the old word for a sudden cry, and the other sense is Private Eye's business. Archimedes leapt out of his bath with this shout on working out how to measure the king's crown.
explanation.definitionFit: Eureka is Greek for I have found it, the cry Archimedes let out in the bath, so the definition describes that shout rather than naming it.

clue.text: Aptness of note the French stuck on high-ranking Republican (9)

blocks.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale, do re mi
le is one of the French words for the
JD Vance, the Republican vice-president

explanation.surface: The French pinning a note of some importance to a senior Republican.
explanation.walkthrough: Aptness of note reads as one phrase meaning noteworthy, and the join is really between the definition and the first piece of the wordplay. Sol-fa notes are the commonest two-letter imports in a grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Relevance is how far a thing bears on the matter in hand, which is aptness in the sense of fitting the occasion.

clue.text: Trump's role now: one who'll get taken down? (8)

blocks.note: the charge the Eye levels at the second term: rule by decree
whatever is dictated is taken down by whoever is listening

explanation.surface: A verdict on the president's current job and a prediction about how it ends.
explanation.walkthrough: Taken down carries both halves of the joke: what a secretary does to dictation, and what a country eventually does to a tyrant. Neither half is wordplay, so there is nothing here to assemble.
explanation.definitionFit: A dictator rules by decree, the role the clue hands Trump, and a dictator is also one who dictates, whose words are taken down.

clue.text: Chastity belt finally accepted by Rugby Union in contest? (6)

indicators.note: Finally points at the end of the word beside it, so only its last letter is taken.
To accept someone is to let them in, so the letter goes inside the pair that accepts it.
In drops what has just been assembled inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: to vie is to contest something, and the word opens after its second letter
RU is the standard short form for Rugby Union, the fifteen-a-side code
the last letter of belt

explanation.surface: A chastity belt's fate settled in some Rugby Union fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: The chastity belt is one image doing two jobs: the first word is the definition, the second hands over a single letter. Contest is the verb vie rather than the noun a match.
explanation.definitionFit: Chastity is one of the virtues, and virtue said of a woman has long carried exactly that sexual sense.

clue.text: Perverse member elected a party leader (5)

indicators.note: Perverse means turned the wrong way about, so the letters just gathered are read back to front.

blocks.note: a leg is a limb, one of the body's members
a candidate who is elected is in

explanation.surface: A contrary MP voted in at the head of his party.
explanation.walkthrough: Member is a limb, not the Commons kind the surface promises, and Private Eye's third sense is in there too. Nigel Farage leads Reform UK, and the papers have long since stopped bothering with his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigel Farage leads Reform UK and is known by his first name alone, which is what lets the name serve as a party leader.

clue.text: Measure crushed by new Tory constitution – a forbidding sign! (2,5)

indicators.note: Something crushed by another thing is squeezed inside it, so these letters go in among the ones doing the crushing.
A thing's constitution is what it is made up of, and naming the make-up releases those letters from their printed order.

blocks.note: n is the short form for new, and the party's four letters follow it into the mix
an en is a printer's measure, the width of the letter it is named after

explanation.surface: A rewritten Tory rulebook squashing some small unit of measurement.
explanation.walkthrough: Constitution is the party's rulebook in the sentence and the make-up of a word in the wordplay. An en is the typesetter's unit that gives the en-dash its name, half the width of an em.
explanation.definitionFit: No entry is the red disc at the mouth of a one-way street, a sign whose whole job is to forbid you to go in.

clue.text: The PM's fight not started – needs energy (6)

indicators.note: A word not started is missing the letter it begins on, so it arrives with its opening gone.

blocks.note: a battle is a fight, entered here without the letter it opens on
E is the physicist's letter for energy, as in Einstein's equation

explanation.surface: A prime minister whose fight has not begun for want of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Clement Attlee led Labour's 1945 landslide and founded the NHS, which is the standing the definite article in The PM leans on. Not started takes off one letter, not the whole first syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement Attlee was Labour's prime minister from 1945 to 1951, so the surname alone answers to The PM.

clue.text: (& 25ac./27ac.)What might well crush Reform's hopes – or working together, even (3)

definitions.text: What might well crush Reform's hopes

indicators.note: To work a lump of dough is to knead it about until it takes a new shape, and letters worked that way come out rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters

explanation.surface: Opposition parties wondering whether cooperation could stop Reform.
explanation.walkthrough: Even sits exactly where an alternate-letters instruction would sit and is fodder instead, which is the one trap here. Reform UK is Nigel Farage's party, top of the polls when this puzzle was set.
explanation.definitionFit: The Green vote is the share going to the Green Party, whose surge is what the clue reckons could deny Reform its majority.

clue.text: Tender "love god", going round bend (5)

definitions.note: Legal tender is a mass noun for the money a country accepts, so it names the currency without taking the plural the answer wears.

indicators.note: Something going round another thing encircles it, so these letters close about the piece named.

blocks.note: Eros is the Greek god of love, and he opens after his first letter
a U-bend is the curved trap under a sink, named for the shape of the letter

explanation.surface: A soppy god of love slowly going mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Going round the bend is the British phrase for losing your mind, and the clue splits it in two: the first half encircles, the second is a letter shaped like a pipe. Tender is the money sense, not the affectionate one the quotation marks push.
explanation.definitionFit: Euros are the notes and coins of the eurozone, legal tender across twenty countries.

clue.text: Drug dealer's raised zero cents – career in the past (5)

indicators.note: Raised lifts the letters up the grid, so in a down entry they are read from the bottom of the assembly to the top.

blocks.note: zero is written as the round O
c is the short form printed against a price in cents
to career is to rush headlong, and the past tense of that verb is what is wanted

explanation.surface: A dealer who has made nothing at all, his working life behind him.
explanation.walkthrough: Career is the verb, to rush headlong, rather than the noun the surface offers, so in the past asks for a tense and not a date. Narco is Latin America's word for a trafficker, clipped off narcotics.
explanation.definitionFit: A narco is a drug trafficker, the Spanish-American term English took over along with the cartels it describes.

clue.text: Parliament: uproar not unfamiliar! (8)

indicators.note: What is unfamiliar is not as you know it, so the little word beside it is re-spelt.

blocks.note: a storm of protest is an uproar
the three letters of not in another order

explanation.surface: An uproar in parliament of a kind everyone has seen before.
explanation.walkthrough: Not unfamiliar reads as one phrase meaning well known, and the two words are doing separate jobs. Stormont is the estate outside Belfast that houses the Northern Ireland Assembly, and stands for it the way Westminster stands for the Commons.
explanation.definitionFit: Stormont is where Northern Ireland's Assembly sits, so the name of the building does duty for the parliament inside it.

clue.text: President wants "land – or bust!" (6)

indicators.note: Bust means broken, and a word broken up does not keep its letters in the order it was printed in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters
two more letters of fodder, the clue's own conjunction

explanation.surface: A president demanding territory and threatening ruin if he does not get it.
explanation.walkthrough: Land or bust is the pioneer's cry heading west, and bust does the shuffling rather than describing a failure. The president after land is the current one; the letters hand over Reagan's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ronald Reagan is the president a first name on its own calls up, so President is doing definition by example.

clue.text: Bind for an ex-PM? (5)

blocks.note: what a cook does to a chicken's legs with string before it goes in the oven
the prime minister who lasted forty-nine days in the autumn of 2022

explanation.surface: Something to tie up a former prime minister with.
explanation.walkthrough: Liz Truss was prime minister for forty-nine days in 2022, outlasted by a tabloid's lettuce, and her surname is also an everyday verb meaning to tie up. The question mark admits that the second half is a name rather than a dictionary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To truss is to bind a bird or a prisoner with rope, and Truss is Liz Truss, briefly prime minister in 2022, so five letters answer to both.

clue.text: One about to read our mag – "Quite something!" (3-6)

blocks.note: the setter works for Private Eye, and the magazine's second word is the piece wanted
whoever is about to read a magazine is the one who opens it

explanation.surface: A reader picking up this fortnight's Private Eye and being startled by it.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops sets for Private Eye, so our mag points at the magazine in the solver's hands. The pieces arrive the other way round from the clue, because what is being described is the mag's opener.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye-opener is something that startles you into seeing straight, which is what quite something says of a revelation.
